module_title: Sourcing and Selecting Quality Raw Materials

lessons.title: Identifying Good Quality Groundnuts: Aflatoxin Prevention and Testing
lessons.body: Aflatoxin is a poison produced by moulds that grow on groundnuts, especially when they are damaged, stored wet, or dried on the ground. In Africa, aflatoxin is a serious health risk and can ruin your peanut butter business because buyers test for it. To prevent aflatoxin, start at harvest: never let nuts touch soil. Dry them on clean mats or tarps, not on bare ground. Dry until moisture is below 10% â you can test with a cheap moisture meter (around $20) or bite a nut: it should crack, not bend. Sort out any shrivelled, discoloured, or mouldy nuts. Mouldy nuts often have a yellow-green or black powdery coating, or they smell musty. Aflatoxin is invisible, so you must also test. Simple field tests include the black light test: aflatoxin glows greenish-yellow under UV light, but this only works for high levels. Better: use a rapid test kit like GIPSA or AgraStrip. These cost about $2-5 per test. For bulk, send a sample to a lab. In many African countries, the standard limit is 10 ppb (parts per billion) for total aflatoxin. If you sell to exporters or processors, they will test. Keep records of your tests. Also, buy from farmers who dry on raised platforms and store in jute bags, not plastic. Never mix good and bad nuts. If you find mould, discard the whole batch â one bad nut can contaminate many. Remember: prevention is cheaper than rejection. Train your suppliers on proper drying and storage. By controlling moisture and damage, you reduce aflatoxin risk by over 90%.

lessons.title: Buying Groundnuts from Local Farmers: Negotiation and Bulk Purchasing
lessons.body: Buying directly from local farmers saves money and builds trust. In many African markets, groundnuts are sold in basins, bags, or tins. A standard bag is 50 kg or 100 kg, but local measures vary. Always weigh before you pay. Use a hanging scale (100 kg capacity, about $30) or a platform scale. Negotiate based on quality and moisture. For example, if a farmer offers 100 kg at $0.80/kg, but moisture is 12%, you will lose weight after drying. Offer $0.70/kg and explain why. Be fair but firm. Bulk purchasing: buy at harvest when prices are lowest. In West Africa, groundnut prices drop 20-30% at harvest. Pool money with other processors to buy a truckload (e.g., 5 tonnes) and get a 10-15% discount. Always inspect before buying: open bags, smell for mustiness, check for live insects, and look for uniform colour. Avoid nuts with black spots or cracked skins. Pay in cash or mobile money on the spot â farmers appreciate quick payment. Build a simple contract: agree on quantity, price, moisture max (10%), and aflatoxin max (10 ppb). Write it in the local language if needed. Keep a record book with farmer names, dates, weights, and prices. Offer a bonus for clean, dry nuts â this encourages quality. For example, pay $0.05/kg extra if moisture is below 9% and no mould. This costs little but improves your supply. Also, consider buying from cooperatives. They aggregate nuts and can meet larger orders. But always test a sample from each lot. Never buy blindly. With good negotiation and bulk buying, you can cut raw material costs by 20-30%.

lessons.title: Storage of Raw Nuts: Preventing Moisture, Pests, and Mold
lessons.body: Proper storage keeps nuts dry, cool, and pest-free. Moisture is the enemy: at above 10% moisture, mould grows and produces aflatoxin. Use airtight containers or jute bags. Never store in plastic bags because they trap moisture. Jute breathes, but it absorbs humidity. Better: use hermetic bags like GrainPro or PICS. These cost about $2-3 each and can hold 50 kg. They block moisture and insects. If hermetic bags are too expensive, use clean metal drums with tight lids. Add a desiccant like silica gel (1 kg per 100 kg nuts) to absorb moisture. Store in a dry, well-ventilated room. Keep bags on pallets or wooden planks, not on the floor. Leave 50 cm gap from walls. Control pests: clean the store before loading. Use traps or approved insecticides like Actellic dust (apply 1 kg per 1000 kg nuts). But never spray directly on nuts for consumption. For rats, use traps or cats. Check stored nuts every 2 weeks. Look for webbing (moth larvae), live insects, or musty smell. If you find insects, sun-dry the nuts for 2-3 hours on a clean mat â this drives out insects. But do not over-dry. Temperature: keep below 25Â°C if possible. In hot climates, store in a shaded area. Never store near fuel, chemicals, or strong smells â nuts absorb odours. Label each bag with date and moisture level. Use first-in, first-out. With good storage, you can keep nuts for 6-12 months with minimal quality loss. Remember: aflatoxin can increase in storage if moisture rises. So monitor with a moisture meter monthly. A $20 meter saves thousands in rejected batches.

lessons.title: Other Nuts for Paste: Cashew, Almond, Sesame, and Their Sourcing
lessons.body: Groundnuts are the cheapest and most common base, but you can make pastes from cashew, almond, and sesame. Cashew nuts: in Africa, major producers are Nigeria, Tanzania, Mozambique, and Ivory Coast. Raw cashew nuts (RCN) are sold in 80 kg bags. Prices vary: $0.80-$1.20/kg for RCN. You must shell and peel them. Shelling is labour-intensive: 1 kg of RCN yields about 250 g of kernels. So kernel cost is 4 times RCN price. Buy RCN from local farmers or cooperatives. Look for uniform size, no black spots, and no rancid smell. Almonds: mostly imported from California or Spain. In Africa, they are expensive â $5-$8/kg. For local paste, blend almonds with groundnuts (20% almond, 80% groundnut) to reduce cost. Source from importers or bulk stores in cities like Nairobi, Lagos, or Accra. Check for freshness: almonds should be crisp, not soft. Sesame seeds: grown in Sudan, Ethiopia, Nigeria, and Tanzania. White sesame is best for paste. Buy in 50 kg bags. Price: $1.00-$1.50/kg. Look for clean, uniform seeds with no sand or stones. Sesame paste (tahini) is made by grinding roasted sesame. You can also blend sesame with groundnuts for a cheaper spread. For all nuts, test for aflatoxin â cashews and almonds are less prone, but sesame can have mould if stored wet. Always buy from reliable suppliers. For cashew, ask for 'raw cashew nuts, grade A' â these have high kernel yield. For sesame, ask for '99% purity, moisture max 6%'. Store all nuts in cool, dry conditions. Start with small quantities to test your market. Many African processors mix groundnut with 10-20% cashew or sesame to create premium products. This adds value and uses local crops.

lessons.title: Costing Raw Materials: Calculating Cost per Kilogram
lessons.body: To know if you are making a profit, you must calculate the true cost per kilogram of usable nuts. Start with the purchase price. For example, you buy 100 kg of groundnuts at $0.80/kg = $80. But you must account for losses: sorting removes 5% (5 kg), drying removes 8% moisture (8 kg), and shelling (if in-shell) removes 30% (30 kg). So usable nuts = 100 - 5 - 8 - 30 = 57 kg. Your cost per usable kg = $80 / 57 = $1.40/kg. That is your real raw material cost. Now add other costs: transport, bags, and labour for sorting. If transport is $10, bags $2, labour $5, total extra $17. New total cost = $97. Cost per kg = $97 / 57 = $1.70/kg. Always use a simple spreadsheet or notebook. Record every purchase: date, supplier, weight, price, moisture, and losses. For mixed nuts, calculate separately. For example, 20 kg cashew at $4/kg = $80, and 80 kg groundnut at $0.80/kg = $64. Total cost $144 for 100 kg mix. But cashew has no shell, groundnut may have 30% shell loss. So usable: cashew 20 kg, groundnut 80*0.7=56 kg, total 76 kg. Cost per kg = $144/76 = $1.89/kg. You also need to add aflatoxin test cost: $3 per test, if you test every 100 kg, that's $0.03/kg. Packaging and labour come later. For pricing, aim for at least 30% gross margin. If cost per kg is $1.70, sell at $2.50/kg or more. Use a simple formula: Selling price = Cost per kg / (1 - desired margin). For 40% margin, price = $1.70 / 0.6 = $2.83/kg. Always recalculate when prices change. Buy in bulk to lower cost per kg. For example, buying 1 tonne instead of 100 kg can reduce price by 15%. Keep records for at least 2 years. This helps you negotiate better and spot trends.

lessons.title: Building Relationships with Reliable Suppliers
lessons.body: Reliable suppliers are the backbone of your peanut butter business. They provide consistent quality, fair prices, and on-time delivery. Start by identifying potential suppliers: local farmers, cooperatives, aggregators, and importers. Visit them in person. Ask about their drying and storage methods. A good supplier dries nuts on raised platforms, stores in jute bags, and tests for aflatoxin. Build trust by paying promptly â within 24 hours if possible. Use mobile money for speed. Offer a fair price, not the lowest. If you squeeze too hard, they will sell to someone else or mix bad nuts. Instead, offer a long-term contract: agree to buy a fixed quantity each month at a set price, with a quality bonus. For example, buy 500 kg per month at $0.75/kg, plus $0.05/kg if moisture is below 9% and aflatoxin below 5 ppb. This gives them security and you quality. Communicate regularly. Call or visit every two weeks. Ask about harvest, weather, and challenges. Share your quality requirements clearly. Provide feedback: if a batch is good, say so. If not, explain why and how to improve. Consider giving small gifts: a bag of cement for a drying floor, or a moisture meter. This invests in their capacity and strengthens loyalty. Keep a supplier scorecard: rate on quality, timeliness, price, and communication. Drop suppliers who repeatedly fail. But give them a chance to improve. Also, diversify: never rely on one supplier. Have at least three. If one fails, you can shift. Join farmer groups or cooperatives â they often have better quality control. Attend local agricultural shows or trade fairs to meet new suppliers. Over time, you can negotiate better terms. A strong relationship means they will warn you about poor harvests and hold stock for you. Treat them as partners, not just vendors. This is how you build a sustainable supply chain.

quiz.q: What is the main health risk from mouldy groundnuts?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is a toxic substance produced by moulds that can cause liver cancer and other health problems.

quiz.q: What moisture level should groundnuts be at for safe storage?
quiz.explanation: Moisture below 10% prevents mould growth and aflatoxin production.

quiz.q: Which tool can help you test moisture in groundnuts?
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter gives a quick reading of water content in nuts.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for aflatoxin?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin glows greenish-yellow under UV light, though it only detects high levels.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid drying groundnuts on bare ground?
options: B) They absorb moisture and mould from soil
quiz.explanation: Soil contact increases moisture and introduces mould spores that produce aflatoxin.

quiz.q: What is a standard bag weight for groundnuts in many African markets?
quiz.explanation: Common bag sizes are 50 kg and 100 kg, but always weigh to confirm.

quiz.q: When are groundnut prices usually lowest?
quiz.explanation: At harvest, supply is high, so prices drop 20-30%.

quiz.q: What should you check when buying groundnuts from a farmer?
quiz.explanation: All these checks help ensure quality and prevent aflatoxin.

quiz.q: What is a fair way to encourage farmers to provide dry, clean nuts?
quiz.explanation: A small bonus per kg for low moisture and no mould motivates farmers to improve quality.

quiz.q: What is a hermetic bag used for?
quiz.explanation: Hermetic bags like GrainPro block moisture and insects, preserving quality.

quiz.q: Why should you not store groundnuts in plastic bags?
quiz.explanation: Plastic bags trap moisture, promoting mould growth and aflatoxin.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored nuts?
quiz.explanation: Regular checks help detect pests or moisture problems early.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find insects in stored nuts?
quiz.explanation: Sun-drying for 2-3 hours drives out insects without chemicals.

quiz.q: What is a good storage practice for bags of nuts?
quiz.explanation: Pallets keep bags off the floor, preventing moisture and pest access.

quiz.q: Which nut is commonly used as a base for alternative pastes in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Cashew, almond, and sesame can all be used, often blended with groundnut.

quiz.q: What is the approximate kernel yield from raw cashew nuts?
quiz.explanation: About 250 g of kernels from 1 kg of raw cashew nuts, so 25% yield.

quiz.q: Why are almonds expensive in Africa?
options: B) They are easy to grow
quiz.explanation: Almonds are mainly imported from California or Spain, adding transport costs.

quiz.q: What is a good quality indicator for sesame seeds?
quiz.explanation: High purity means less sand, stones, and foreign matter.

quiz.q: What is tahini?
quiz.explanation: Tahini is a paste made from ground roasted sesame seeds.

quiz.q: When blending nuts, what is a common ratio to reduce cost?
quiz.explanation: Using 20% almond with 80% groundnut lowers cost while adding flavour.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calculating cost per kilogram of usable nuts?
options: B) Determine purchase price and weight
quiz.explanation: Start with the price paid and the weight bought to find base cost.

quiz.q: If you buy 100 kg groundnuts at $0.80/kg and lose 30% to shelling, what is the cost per usable kg (ignoring other losses)?
quiz.explanation: Usable weight = 70 kg; cost = $80/70 = $1.14/kg.

quiz.q: Why should you add aflatoxin test cost to your raw material cost?
options: A) It is a legal requirement
B) It ensures safety and affects total cost
quiz.explanation: Testing adds to cost but is necessary to avoid rejected batches and health risks.

quiz.q: What is a simple formula to set selling price with a desired margin?
options: A) Price = Cost per kg + Margin
B) Price = Cost per kg / (1 - Margin)
C) Price = Cost per kg * Margin
D) Price = Cost per kg - Margin
quiz.explanation: This formula ensures the margin is a percentage of the selling price.

quiz.q: Why keep records of raw material purchases for at least 2 years?
options: A) To negotiate better and spot trends
quiz.explanation: Historical data helps you understand price patterns and improve buying decisions.

quiz.q: What is a key trait of a reliable supplier?
quiz.explanation: Consistent quality means you can trust their nuts for your production.

quiz.q: How can you build trust with a supplier?
quiz.explanation: Prompt payment shows respect and encourages loyalty.

quiz.q: What is a good way to motivate suppliers to maintain quality?
options: A) Offer a long-term contract with quality bonus
quiz.explanation: A contract with bonus gives security and incentive for quality.

quiz.q: Why should you diversify your suppliers?
options: A) To avoid relying on one
quiz.explanation: Having at least three suppliers ensures you can shift if one fails.

quiz.q: What is a supplier scorecard used for?
options: A) Rating suppliers on quality, timeliness, price, communication
quiz.explanation: A scorecard helps you objectively evaluate and compare suppliers.
